Recursive Harness Self-Improvement

Recursive Harness Self-Improvement for Frontier Reasoning Data Synthesis

Wenlong Zhang Affiliation: University of Science and Technology of China    Zhengbo Jiao Affiliation: Shanghai University of Finance and Economics    Chenxu Zhang    Lekang Jiang Affiliation: University of Cambridge    SiYuan Ma Affiliation: Nanyang Technological University    Qituan Zhang Affiliation: EPIC Lab, Shanghai Jiao Tong University Affiliation: Fudan University    Guo Chen Affiliation: EPIC Lab, Shanghai Jiao Tong University Affiliation: University of Electronic Science and Technology of China *Equal Contribution.†Corresponding Author.    Linfeng Zhang Affiliation: Imperial College London
Abstract

Generating progressively harder reasoning problems requires synthesis procedures that adapt as the task distribution evolves. Existing task-level recursion reuses generated problems as seeds but leaves the construction harness unchanged. We present task–harness co-evolution, a framework for recursive harness self-improvement (RSI) in reasoning-data synthesis. Online self-improvement converts intermediate solver failures into reusable skills during generation. Post-task self-improvement revises skills, prompts, and workflows after each batch, adopting candidates only when they generate harder valid tasks within a bounded cost increase. Model weights and verification criteria remain fixed. Across mathematics, coding, and science, mean solver accuracy decreases from 100.0% to 54.8% over fourteen evolution rounds. Ablations show that combining both update schedules produces harder tasks than fixed-harness recursion or either schedule alone. The resulting data improves downstream SFT and GRPO performance. In particular, a 27B student fine-tuned on 10K synthesized mathematics examples achieves 62.5% mean-16 accuracy on APEX, competitive with selected frontier-model references. These results support adapting the synthesis harness alongside the tasks to generate increasingly challenging data with downstream training value.

1 Introduction

Advances in mathematical, scientific, and coding reasoning depend on a continuing supply of high-quality, challenging problems. OpenMathInstruct-2 demonstrates the value of synthetic data for mathematical reasoning training (Toshniwal et al., 2025), while FrontierMath highlights the need for problems that distinguish advanced reasoning capabilities (Glazer et al., 2024). As model capabilities improve, however, a static dataset cannot adapt its difficulty. Increasing dataset size alone does not ensure that the synthesis procedure can construct progressively harder reasoning problems. Here, the synthesis harness comprises reusable skills, prompts, and workflows that turn a seed into a verified problem. Adapting these components offers a way to respond to changing solver weaknesses.

Existing synthesis methods progress from instruction expansion to recursive task evolution. Self-Instruct generates instructions from model outputs (Wang et al., 2023), and WizardLM increases instruction complexity through predefined operators (Xu et al., 2024). RST recursively reuses verified terminal tasks as seeds, demonstrating the potential of task-level recursion under a largely fixed synthesis procedure (Li et al., 2026). Yet evolving the tasks alone leaves their reusable construction skills and workflows unchanged. Autodata and DataFoundry instead optimize data-generating agents and data-preparation runtimes (Kulikov et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026). Together, these directions motivate adapting the generation procedure alongside its evolving task distribution. This raises a specific question for recursive synthesis: can the generation procedure improve as its own outputs become the inputs to subsequent rounds?

To address this limitation, we present task–harness co-evolution, a framework that improves reasoning tasks and their synthesis harness together (Figure 1). Verified tasks seed the next round, while generation feedback guides two complementary update schedules. Online self-improvement converts intermediate solver failures into reusable skills before generation finishes. Post-task self-improvement uses completed-batch feedback to revise skills, prompts, and workflows. Candidate harnesses are compared with the online snapshot before adoption, with rollback when revisions do not satisfy the validity, difficulty, and cost criteria. Model weights and verification logic remain fixed, so adaptation occurs in the generation procedure rather than the model. Candidate evaluation uses the harness containing online updates as its baseline. If all batch-level candidates are rejected, online skills are retained for the next generation round.

Experiments across mathematics, coding, and science demonstrate sustained difficulty growth and downstream training value (Figure 2). Fixed-solver accuracy falls from 100.0% to 54.8% over fourteen evolution rounds, while the synthesized data improves both SFT and GRPO performance. With only 10K mathematics examples, a 27B student reaches 62.5% on APEX, competitive with selected frontier-model references on this benchmark. Our main contributions are as follows:

  1. 1.

    Task–Harness Co-Evolution. We introduce a synthesis framework that recursively evolves reasoning tasks and their generation harness together, extending task-only recursion to adaptive construction procedures.

  2. 2.

    Online and Post-Task Self-Improvement. We combine immediate skill updates during generation with batch-level harness revision, candidate evaluation, and rollback under fixed verification criteria and bounded cost growth.

  3. 3.

    Difficulty Growth and Training Utility. We show that the combined update schedules produce harder tasks than fixed-harness recursion and either schedule alone, while the resulting data improves downstream reasoning through both SFT and GRPO.

2 Related Work

Frontier Reasoning in Science.

The progress of large language models has made the difficulty frontier of reasoning a moving target. Mathematical and scientific reasoning benchmarks such as MATH, GPQA, and FrontierMath progressively test competition-level, graduate-level, and exceptionally difficult reasoning (Hendrycks et al., 2021; Rein et al., 2024; Glazer et al., 2024). Humanity’s Last Exam and SciCode extend this evaluation to broad academic knowledge and research-oriented scientific coding (Phan et al., 2025; Tian et al., 2024), while FrontierScience explicitly evaluates expert-level scientific tasks (Wang et al., 2026). Complementary solver systems such as AlphaGeometry, AlphaProof, DeepSeek-R1, and AlphaEvolve combine language models with formal verification, reinforcement learning, or automated search to tackle increasingly complex mathematical and scientific problems (Trinh et al., 2024; Hubert et al., 2026; DeepSeek-AI, 2025; Novikov et al., 2025). Together, these benchmarks and systems show that progress requires problems that expose the remaining capabilities of strong solvers. They also motivate synthesis methods that can generate valid and informative challenges as the reasoning frontier moves.

Reasoning Data Synthesis.

Synthetic-data methods have evolved from instruction bootstrapping to feedback-driven and recursive task construction. Self-Instruct samples and filters model-generated instructions, while WizardLM applies predefined operators to increase instruction complexity (Wang et al., 2023; Xu et al., 2024). OpenMathInstruct-2 further studies large-scale math question–solution synthesis and its effect on downstream training (Toshniwal et al., 2025). Other methods improve reasoning data through self-training or self-play: STaR filters generated rationales by correctness, ReSTEM iterates between generation and model updating, and Absolute Zero and R-Zero use verifiable feedback to couple task proposal with reasoning improvement (Zelikman et al., 2022; Singh et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2025). Auto Evol-Instruct learns instruction-evolution strategies from prior trajectories (Zeng et al., 2024). BenchEvolver and Recursive Synthetic Terminal Tasks (RST) make recursion explicit by reusing solutions or verified task bundles as seeds for subsequent task generation (Wu et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026). This line of work shows that task or seed recursion can expand the difficulty frontier. Our approach further adapts the construction skills and workflow alongside the evolving task distribution.

Harness Evolution and RSI.

Another line of work treats an agent’s surrounding program as an optimization target. ADAS generates and evaluates code-defined agent designs, while AFlow searches over code-represented workflows using execution feedback (Hu et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025b). Recursive self-improvement methods further evolve the improvement procedure itself: Promptbreeder evolves mutation prompts, STOP recursively improves a code optimizer, and the Darwin Gödel Machine maintains an archive of validated self-modifications (Fernando et al., 2024; Zelikman et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025a). Recent harness-oriented systems study prompt-level revision, end-to-end harness optimization, and meta-agents that improve both a task agent and its improvement procedure (Lee et al., 2026a; Lee et al., 2026b; Zhang et al., 2026). Autodata optimizes a data-scientist scaffold using generation and solver feedback, whereas DataFoundry evolves an executable data-preparation runtime through pilot-set diagnosis and component-level adapters (Kulikov et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026).

3 Harness-Level Self-Evolution

We recursively synthesize tasks with a fixed language model and an adaptive harness (Figure 3). After one-time initialization (Stage 1), each round combines two update schedules. Online self-improvement (Stage 2) turns intermediate solver failures into immediately usable construction skills during generation. Post-task self-improvement (Stage 3) revises, evaluates, and selects the harness after the batch ends. Algorithm 1 (Appendix A) gives the complete procedure.

3.1 Problem Formulation and Initialization

A harness comprises reusable construction skills ℒ\mathcal{L}, role prompts PP, workflow WW, and verification/revision placements ρV,ρR\rho_{V},\rho_{R}:

H=(ℒ,P,W,ρV,ρR).H=(\mathcal{L},P,W,\rho_{V},\rho_{R}). (1)

Model weights, verifier implementation, and final validity criteria remain fixed. Online adaptation changes the skill component; batch-level optimization can revise all components, including when verification and revision are invoked.

Starting from NN verified seeds 𝒯0\mathcal{T}_{0}, round nn constructs 𝒯n+1\mathcal{T}_{n+1} from 𝒯n\mathcal{T}_{n} using a working copy of HnH_{n}. Each seed chain retains its latest valid, completed QA. An unsuccessful attempt preserves the predecessor, so every round contains one task per original seed. We do not select the hardest ancestor retrospectively; failed attempts remain in the logs and cost accounting.

CgenC_{\mathrm{gen}} includes Director, generation, verification, revision, and online-update calls, including failed attempts. We prioritize difficulty subject to validity and bounded cost growth, allowing additional computation for harder tasks. Repeated solver attempts are not independent evolution runs.

Stage 1: data curation and initialization.

Before selecting seeds or distilling skills, we screen candidate seeds and source passages from coding, mathematics, and science datasets, papers, and web documents for duplicates and benchmark overlap. Duplicate seed families remain within one evolution/held-out split; benchmark items and solutions are isolated from the generation agents. An acquisition model extracts reusable task transformations using the fields intent, method, difficulty_effect, and tool_hint. Screened skills, initial prompts, and workflow form H0H_{0}. Skill examples and training exports are checked again for overlap, since input screening alone does not exclude contamination introduced during synthesis (Toshniwal et al., 2025). Appendix B details curation and evaluation procedures.

3.2 Online self-improvement

The Director selects skills and controls Extend, Revise, and Verify until Finish or budget exhaustion. The diagram shows the initial ordering, which batch-level optimization may revise. During verification, the generating model also attempts the intermediate QA qn,tq_{n,t}. A solver failure attributable to a reasoning weakness on a valid QA yields a trace zn,tmissz^{\mathrm{miss}}_{n,t}. The Meta Agent converts this weakness into a reusable construction transformation, rather than an answer to that particular QA:

ℒn,t+1=Admit⁡(ℒn,t,Metas⁡(qn,t,zn,tmiss,Γs)).\mathcal{L}_{n,t+1}=\operatorname{Admit}\!\left(\mathcal{L}_{n,t},\operatorname{Meta}_{s}(q_{n,t},z^{\mathrm{miss}}_{n,t};\Gamma_{s})\right). (3)

Γs\Gamma_{s} specifies applicability, reusability, and supporting evidence. Admit incorporates qualifying skills; invalid QA, incorrect reference answers, and tool failures instead trigger repair.

The next Director call reads the updated library, making the skill available to the unfinished task and remaining tasks in the same batch. This avoids delaying reusable failure feedback until all tasks finish. At the batch boundary, we freeze the resulting harness as HnonlineH_{n}^{\mathrm{online}}, the comparison baseline and fallback for the next optimization step. Admitted skills need not increase task difficulty.

3.3 Post-task self-improvement

Post-task self-improvement starts after the task batch completes or its generation budget expires. We treat revision and candidate evaluation as a single outer optimization loop, using completed batches to assess effects beyond an individual failure trace. This organization follows feedback-driven harness search (Lee et al., 2026b; Lee et al., 2026a); we evaluate task validity, difficulty, and generation cost.

Feedback and revision.

Stage 3’s production row recaps Stage 2 rather than generating again. After batch termination, in-loop tests of retained tasks 𝒯n+1\mathcal{T}_{n+1} produce scores ℰn\mathcal{E}_{n} and failure traces. Process & filter prepares these signals and run logs for the Meta Agent without excluding failed attempts from evaluation or costs. The Meta Agent first updates skills in a copy of HnonlineH_{n}^{\mathrm{online}}, yielding H^n\widehat{H}_{n}. It then uses execution logs 𝒵n\mathcal{Z}_{n}, operational metrics ℳn\mathcal{M}_{n}, and human-specified goal gg and constraints Γ\Gamma to propose a candidate:

Δ​Hn(j)\displaystyle\Delta H_{n}^{(j)} =Metah⁡(H^n,𝒵n,ℳn,ℰn,Γ,g,ℛ<j),\displaystyle=\operatorname{Meta}_{h}(\widehat{H}_{n},\mathcal{Z}_{n},\mathcal{M}_{n},\mathcal{E}_{n};\Gamma,g,\mathcal{R}_{<j}), (4)
Hn′(j)\displaystyle H_{n}^{\prime(j)} =Apply⁡(H^n,Δ​Hn(j)).\displaystyle=\operatorname{Apply}(\widehat{H}_{n},\Delta H_{n}^{(j)}).

The goal and constraints are specified in advance. Allowed edits include adding, revising, or removing skills; changing prompts and workflow; and repositioning Verify and Revise. Verifier logic cannot change. Each proposal starts from H^n\widehat{H}_{n} and can use previous rejection reports ℛ<j\mathcal{R}_{<j}; rejected edits do not accumulate automatically.

Candidate evaluation and selection.

We freeze a shared cohort SnS_{n} of current retained tasks as evaluation inputs. Each candidate and Ho=HnonlineH_{o}=H_{n}^{\mathrm{online}} independently synthesize one further round from SnS_{n}, with identical model/tool settings and resource ceilings. We compare the new outputs, not previously recorded scores of SnS_{n}. Each side uses its own library and online adaptation in isolation; evaluation updates and outputs do not alter the production snapshots or task chains. Let Q⁡(H)Q(H) be the fraction of new final candidates passing validity before fallback, with missing candidates counted as invalid. The Critic accepts a candidate only if

A(H′,Ho)=𝕀[\displaystyle A(H^{\prime},H_{o})=\mathbb{I}\bigl[ H′∈ℋΓ,Q(H′)≥Q(Ho),\displaystyle H^{\prime}\in\mathcal{H}_{\Gamma},\ Q(H^{\prime})\geq Q(H_{o}), (5)
A¯​(H′)<A¯​(Ho),\displaystyle\bar{A}(H^{\prime})<\bar{A}(H_{o}),
C¯gen​(H′)≤min⁡{1+1.5​(rD−1), 1.5}\displaystyle\bar{C}_{\mathrm{gen}}(H^{\prime})\leq\min\{1+1.5(r_{D}-1),\,1.5\}
⋅C¯gen(Ho)],\displaystyle}{\displaystyle\cdot\bar{C}_{\mathrm{gen}}(H_{o})\bigr],

where ℋΓ\mathcal{H}_{\Gamma} enforces edit and fixed resource limits. The prescribed cost allowance is 1.5 times the relative difficulty gain, capped at a 50% increase over the online baseline. Thus a 20% difficulty gain permits at most 30% higher cost. This difficulty-first empirical gate requires no validity decrease; it guarantees neither improved cost efficiency nor improvement on unseen tasks. Appendix B specifies cohort composition, evaluation budgets, boundary cases, and accounting.

The first accepted candidate becomes Hn+1H_{n+1}. Input tasks and baseline results stay fixed across the initial proposal and at most two retries (three candidate evaluations). After three rejections, Hn+1=HnonlineH_{n+1}=H_{n}^{\mathrm{online}}: all post-task edits, including post-batch skill updates, are discarded. Online skills and rejection logs remain. Exhausting the evaluation budget without acceptance also retains the online snapshot; incomplete probes cannot pass. We archive accepted and online-only fallback versions with distinct statuses; both use 𝒯n+1\mathcal{T}_{n+1} to seed the next round. Final held-out evaluations never inform updates or candidate selection.

4 Experiments

4.1 Experimental Setup

We evaluate synthesis across mathematics, coding, and science using DeepSeek-V4-Pro as the fixed solver; difficulty is measured by mean accuracy over four attempts per task. Downstream experiments train Qwen3.5-4B Thinking with GRPO and Qwen3.5-35B-A3B and Qwen3.8-27B with SFT. We evaluate the benchmarks in Tables 2 and 2 using MathArena (Dekoninck et al., 2026) and report mean-16 accuracy. Within each training comparison, baselines share hyperparameters. Model assignments, training configurations, and evaluation details are consolidated in Appendix F.

4.2 Difficulty Progression

We evolve 150 seed chains for 14 rounds, with 50 per domain. Round r=0r=0 denotes the original seeds; unsuccessful attempts retain the latest valid task. Overall accuracy equally weights domains; repeated solver attempts are not independent evolution runs.

Overall accuracy decreases from 100.0% to 54.8% by round 14, a 45.2-point decline. Domain accuracies reach 50.0%, 58.5%, and 56.0%, respectively (Figure 4). The decline occurs in every domain under a fixed cohort, rather than through a change in domain composition.

4.3 Online and Post-task Self-Improvement Ablations

Four configurations share 50 initial seeds and harness: Task-only keeps the harness fixed; Online only updates skills during generation; Post-task only updates the harness after each batch, including skill revisions and candidate evaluation; Full combines both schedules (Sections 3.2–3.3). All retain QA verification, independently of the harness acceptance gate.

Online only reaches 67.0% at round 14, versus 73.5% for Task-only, but regresses from 64.5% at round 10. The curve does not identify skill quality as the cause. Post-task only reaches 59.0%, while Full reaches 50.0%: improvements of 9.0 points over Post-task only and 23.5 points over Task-only (Figure 5). These results support complementary update schedules, without isolating the contribution of candidate screening within post-task optimization.

Full also improves over Online only by 17.0 points at round 14. Together, the two comparisons support complementary roles: online adaptation makes failure-derived skills available within the current batch, while post-task optimization can reconsider the accumulated library and the workflow that uses it. The combined configuration benefits from both opportunities. These gains do not imply monotonic improvement under either schedule or benefits from every new skill.

Late-round behavior further distinguishes the schedules. From round 10 to round 14, Full reduces solver accuracy from 57.0% to 50.0%, while Post-task only improves from 63.5% to 59.0%. Both continue making tasks harder as Online only regresses. This pattern is consistent with a benefit from revisiting the accumulated harness, although the finite trajectory does not establish eventual convergence for any configuration.

4.4 Harness Transfer and Generation Cost

Frozen-harness transfer.

Both snapshots, including their skill libraries, remain frozen on 50 mathematics seeds not used to evolve or select H14H_{14}. Subscripts identify harness versions, not evaluation rounds. After ten recursive generation rounds, H14H_{14} yields 52.0% solver accuracy versus 70.0% for H0H_{0} (Figure 6a), supporting transfer to these held-out seeds without further harness updates. Because both harnesses restart from the same seeds, the 18.0-point gap cannot be attributed to starting H14H_{14} from its own harder terminal tasks. Freezing the snapshots also prevents new online or post-task adaptations during this comparison. The result supports reuse of the evolved generation procedure beyond its original chains, while evaluating transfer within mathematics under the same solver rather than across solvers or domains.

Generation-operator cost.

We divide each round’s Extend/Revise/Verify fees by 50 reasoning seeds; costs are not cumulative. Full costs slightly more at rounds 2 and 4, but less at every reported round from 6 onward. At round 14, accuracy is 50.0% versus 73.5% for Task-only, while cost is $1.065 versus $1.332 per seed, a 20.0% reduction (Figure 6b). Excluding Director, skill-update, and search overhead, this measure is narrower than C¯gen\bar{C}_{\mathrm{gen}} in Eq. (2) and cannot show total savings.

4.5 Downstream Training Utility

GRPO on a 4B student.

We train Qwen3.5-4B Thinking on 10K examples per data configuration. Our data yields the highest accuracy on all four benchmarks (Table 2). The unweighted average reaches 62.7%, versus 58.4% for Qwen3.5-4B Thinking and 59.5% for IQC, the strongest data comparison by overall accuracy. The gains over the checkpoint are 4.0, 4.8, 3.4, and 5.1 points on APEX Shortlist, HMMT, LCB, and SciBench, respectively. Thus the overall improvement accompanies gains in every evaluated domain. The strongest alternative differs by benchmark: OpenMathInstruct-2 leads the data comparisons on HMMT, OpenCodeReasoning on LCB, and IQC on APEX Shortlist and SciBench. Our data exceeds each of these scores.

SFT on a 35B student.

Our data leads on all four benchmarks (Table 2); the unweighted average is 55.7%, exceeding both the checkpoint and MMIQC/IQC by 4.6 points using the displayed scores. Together with GRPO, this supports utility under both training procedures. OpenMathInstruct-2 and MMIQC/IQC improve APEX Shortlist and HMMT but reduce LCB accuracy, whereas OpenCodeReasoning improves LCB but reduces the three mathematics scores. Our configuration improves all four scores, with gains of 3.1, 5.4, 5.8, and 4.3 points, respectively. The aggregate gain therefore reflects improvements across both mathematics and coding. These comparisons characterize the evaluated data mixtures and training settings, rather than a universal ranking of source datasets.

APEX performance with a 27B student.

Qwen3.8-27B improves from 56.3% to 62.5% mean-16 accuracy on APEX 2025, a 6.2-point gain using the displayed scores (Figure 2b; Appendix C). We evaluate all compared models with MathArena (Dekoninck et al., 2026), using 16 attempts per problem. Comparisons do not imply equal training or inference costs.

Scope of the evidence.

Isolating the downstream contribution of harness evolution requires matched-token training on our fixed-harness and evolved-harness data. Total evolution cost, candidate validity, fallback rates, and independent-run uncertainty remain unreported. Transfer to held-out seeds and lower operator costs do not establish transfer to independent solvers or end-to-end compute efficiency.

5 Conclusion

We introduced task–harness co-evolution for progressively harder reasoning-data synthesis. The framework combines Online self-improvement from intermediate solver failures with Post-task self-improvement of skills, prompts, and workflows. Candidate evaluation and reversible snapshots govern batch-level adoption, while verifier logic remains fixed. Across mathematics, coding, and science, fixed-solver accuracy falls from 100.0% to 54.8% by round 14. The update ablation further shows a 23.5-point accuracy reduction relative to fixed-harness recursion at round 14, supporting the combination of online and batch-level adaptation. Downstream SFT and GRPO results establish training utility across the evaluated benchmarks; a 27B student fine-tuned on 10K mathematics examples reaches 62.5% mean-16 accuracy on APEX. These findings identify the synthesis harness as a useful target of recursive improvement. Frozen evaluation on shared held-out seeds further shows that the evolved harness can generate harder tasks without additional adaptation. This result links the difficulty gains to a reusable generation procedure, beyond the particular task chains used to evolve it.

Future work should compare fixed- and evolved-harness data under matched training tokens, and measure total generation cost, candidate validity, and difficulty transfer to independent solvers.

AI use statement

Generative AI tools assisted with synthetic data generation, code development, experiment-log organization and analysis, manuscript drafting, and language editing. The authors are responsible for independently verifying all algorithmic claims, references, experimental results, and final manuscript content.

Appendix A Complete Evolution Procedure

Algorithm 1 integrates Online self-improvement and Post-task self-improvement. The latter includes post-batch skill updates, joint revision, candidate evaluation, and bounded retries. The online snapshot is the default next-round harness; only an accepted candidate replaces it. Thus three rejections discard all batch-level changes without removing skills acquired during generation.

Appendix B Method Protocol Details

Curation and overlap control.

We freeze benchmark versions before screening both candidate seeds and skill-distillation sources. Normalized exact duplicates and confirmed benchmark overlaps are removed; lexical and semantic matching flags near-duplicates and paraphrases for review. Shared concepts alone do not constitute overlap. Duplicate seed families remain within a single split when forming evolution and held-out pools. Only retained materials enter the generation and acquisition agents; benchmark items and solutions remain confined to the isolated overlap checker. Source identifiers and filtering decisions are retained for auditing. Distilled skill examples and final training exports undergo further overlap checks. Training-export deduplication does not change the fixed seed cohort used for difficulty measurement. These rules specify the curation protocol; they do not establish the absence of contamination without the corresponding audit records.

Skill representation and attribution.

Each skill describes a reusable question-construction transformation. The field intent identifies the reasoning capability to probe; method describes the transformation; difficulty_effect states its intended effect on difficulty; and tool_hint identifies supporting tools or procedures. Skill admission checks applicability, reusability, and supporting evidence. A solver miss must be distinguished from an invalid problem, an incorrect reference answer, or a tool failure, which instead calls for repair. Trace and skill identifiers preserve provenance and prevent duplicate processing. The operators Metas\operatorname{Meta}_{s} and Metah\operatorname{Meta}_{h} denote skill-update and harness-revision roles; they need not use different underlying models.

Isolated candidate evaluation.

After the batch, freeze the shared gate cohort SnS_{n}: 50 current retained tasks each from mathematics, coding, and science (150 in total). This gate cohort is specified separately from the 50-seed cohorts used to report the update ablation, frozen-harness transfer, and operator cost. The online baseline and each candidate synthesize one additional round from this set under matched model/tool settings and resource ceilings. Inputs and once-computed baseline results remain fixed through the initial candidate and at most two retries (three candidate evaluations). Each probe copies the relevant snapshot, retains its full skill library, and follows the same online-adaptation protocol. Probe-time skills are neither shared nor written back; probe outputs do not advance production. Equal libraries are needed only to isolate workflow edits in an ablation. This current-task selection is not a held-out generalization test. Each proposal starts from a fresh copy of H^\widehat{H} plus rejection reports, without accumulating rejected edits.

Acceptance metrics and budget.

The gate uses 150 shared seed chains (50 per domain) and four solver attempts per retained output, or 600 outcomes per harness. Mean accuracy gives each seed equal weight. The 600 outcomes are clustered within 150 tasks, not independent tasks. Relative difficulty is the ratio of the two cohort accuracies; a decrease from 0.60 to 0.50 gives rD=1.2r_{D}=1.2. Equation (5) requires strictly lower accuracy and no decrease in new-candidate validity. The cost-growth coefficient and relative cap are both 1.5, fixed before search. In this example, a candidate may cost up to 1.30 times the baseline. These are engineering preferences for bounded spending, not statistically calibrated thresholds or a claim of optimal cost efficiency.

If A¯​(Ho)=0\bar{A}(H_{o})=0, no candidate can achieve strictly lower accuracy. If A¯​(H′)=0<A¯​(Ho)\bar{A}(H^{\prime})=0<\bar{A}(H_{o}), apply the 1.5 cost cap directly without dividing by zero. More generally, after checking the strict accuracy condition, the cost test is equivalently

C¯gen​(H′)\displaystyle\bar{C}_{\mathrm{gen}}(H^{\prime}) ≤1.5​C¯gen​(Ho),\displaystyle\leq 1.5\bar{C}_{\mathrm{gen}}(H_{o}),
C¯gen​(H′)​A¯​(H′)\displaystyle\bar{C}_{\mathrm{gen}}(H^{\prime})\bar{A}(H^{\prime}) ≤C¯gen​(Ho)​[1.5​A¯​(Ho)−0.5​A¯​(H′)].\displaystyle\leq\bar{C}_{\mathrm{gen}}(H_{o})\bigl[1.5\bar{A}(H_{o})-0.5\bar{A}(H^{\prime})\bigr].

Difficulty uses the latest valid completed task from every original seed chain. In contrast, QQ measures new-candidate validity before fallback; missing new candidates count as invalid. This prevents retaining valid predecessors from masking failed synthesis.

Input tasks, solver settings, absolute generation/evaluation ceilings, and baseline results stay fixed throughout a search. The relative cost allowance does not raise these ceilings. Stop at the first accepted candidate, after three rejected candidates, or when the evaluation budget expires; without acceptance, retain the online snapshot. With one baseline and three complete candidate probes, difficulty scoring uses at most 2,400 solver attempts, excluding generation-time verification and other calls. Incomplete probes cannot be accepted.

Cost accounting and reporting.

The generation cost in Eq. (2) includes Director, construction, revision, verification, and online skill-update calls, including unsuccessful attempts. Total evolution cost additionally includes initialization, post-batch evaluation and updates, and all candidate-search calls, including rejected proposals and baseline evaluations. Divide by the original seed count rather than the number of newly successful generations. Evaluation performed solely for final reporting is accounted for separately and never feeds back into updates. Cost comparisons should report difficulty and absolute cost separately, with consistent pricing or token accounting, and include a matched-total-budget comparison. Passing the gate does not establish lower absolute cost, lower cost per unit of difficulty, or lower total evolution cost. Absolute limits remain necessary because the relative cap only compares a candidate with its current online baseline.

Version history and fallback.

The archive ℬ\mathcal{B} stores complete harness and task snapshots, parent identifiers, acceptance status, evaluation records, rejection reports, and costs. Accepted candidates create new accepted versions; three rejected candidates produce an online-only version retaining HonlineH^{\mathrm{online}}. The latter does not represent a Critic-accepted batch-level improvement. Both outcomes use the retained tasks as seeds for the next round and preserve reproducible rollback points.

Appendix C Additional APEX Training and Reference Results

Before and after SFT.

The Qwen3.8-27B starting checkpoint achieves 56.3% on APEX, while SFT on 10K synthesized mathematics examples reaches 62.5% (Table 3). The improvement is 6.2 percentage points, computed from the displayed scores. Both results use mean-16 accuracy. This within-checkpoint comparison complements the 35B training-data comparison in Table 2; it measures the observed training gain, rather than isolating the contribution of harness evolution to that gain.

Selected reference models.

Table 4 compares our 27B SFT model with selected reference models. We evaluate every listed model ourselves on APEX 2025 using the MathArena framework [Dekoninck et al., 2026]. Our model uses 10K mathematics examples for SFT. Each reported score averages 16 attempts per problem (mean-16), following the APEX protocol [Dekoninck et al., 2025], rather than measuring pass@16. Scores are displayed to one decimal, with gaps calculated from the displayed scores. The 3.1-point gap to Kimi K3 (Think) describes point estimates, not statistical equivalence. The ordering concerns only the listed models, and equal evaluation counts do not imply equal compute.

Appendix D Numerical Difficulty and Ablation Results

Tables 5 and 6 retain all reported values underlying Figures 4 and 5. The overall accuracy is recomputed from three equally weighted domains. The four solver evaluations used in the domain experiment are not independent evolution runs; no run-level uncertainty is inferred from these aggregate values.

Appendix E Frozen-Harness and Cost Evaluation

Frozen-harness protocol.

The two snapshots start from the same 50 mathematics seeds, which did not participate in the evolution or selection of H14H_{14}. Skills, prompts, workflows, and verification/revision placements remain frozen; only the tasks evolve. Table 7 reports the fresh generation trajectory, whose round index is distinct from the harness version. These seeds are separate from the reasoning cohort used for the operator-cost experiment. The H0H_{0} round-10 accuracy of 70.0% belongs to this experiment and is not the 72.5% task-only entry from the update ablation.

Operator-cost scope.

For each reported round rr, the denominator is the original 50 reasoning seeds, rather than the number of newly successful tasks:

C¯ERV(r)=CExtend(r)+CRevise(r)+CVerify(r)50.\bar{C}_{\mathrm{ERV}}^{(r)}=\frac{C_{\mathrm{Extend}}^{(r)}+C_{\mathrm{Revise}}^{(r)}+C_{\mathrm{Verify}}^{(r)}}{50}.

This measure includes only the reported generation-operator fees. It excludes Director calls, online skill updates, post-task updates, candidate search and evaluation (including rejected candidates), initialization, and standalone reporting evaluations. It is therefore not the full generation-cost numerator used for harness acceptance or an estimate of total search cost. Values are for individual rounds; unreported rounds are not interpolated or included in a cumulative sum. No cost is assigned to the starting seed row.

At round 14, Full reduces solver accuracy by 23.5 percentage points and operator cost by $0.267 per seed (20.0%). The cost difference is computed from the reported three-decimal fees. The earlier round-2 and round-4 operator costs are respectively 2.0% and 2.9% higher for Full. These results do not quantify the cost of obtaining H14H_{14} or establish matched-total-budget superiority. Raw billing records, pricing schedules, call counts, and independent-run uncertainty are needed for a full cost audit.

Appendix F Experimental Setup

F.1 Models, Benchmarks, and Evaluation

Synthesis models.

Director, Extend, and Revise use DeepSeek-V4-Pro. Verify uses Qwen3.8-Max, DeepSeek-V4-Pro, and GPT-5.6; the meta-agent uses DeepSeek-V4-Pro and GPT-5.6. All listed synthesis and meta-agent models run with Thinking enabled.

Evaluation and student models.

We use DeepSeek-V4-Pro as the fixed solver for difficulty evaluation. Students are Qwen3.5-4B Thinking for GRPO and Qwen3.5-35B-A3B and Qwen3.8-27B for SFT.

Benchmarks.

We evaluate on APEX/Shortlist, HMMT, LiveCodeBench v6 [Jain et al., 2024], and SciBench [Wang et al., 2024]. GRPO and SFT use HMMT February 2025 and 2026, respectively. The evaluated LCB v6 and SciBench sets contain 454 and 695 problems, respectively.

Evaluation protocols.

We use the MathArena evaluation framework [Dekoninck et al., 2026]. All APEX scores, including those of the reference models, are obtained in our own evaluations. Difficulty averages four solver attempts per task; lower accuracy is harder. All four GRPO benchmarks use mean-16 accuracy: the mean correctness across 16 test attempts per problem, not pass@16. Higher downstream accuracy is better; SFT protocols are specified alongside the results.

Datasets and baselines.

We compare with OpenMathInstruct-2 [Toshniwal et al., 2025], OpenCodeReasoning [Ahmad et al., 2025], and recursive IQC/MMIQC [Liu et al., 2024]; GRPO also includes WildSci [Liu et al., 2026] and MetaMath [Yu et al., 2023].

F.2 Training Configuration

Controlled training comparisons.

The 4B GRPO and both SFT experiments use verl on 16 NVIDIA H20 GPUs, with shared hyperparameters across datasets within each comparison. GRPO uses 10K training examples per data configuration. The 35B comparison uses 12K examples per configuration (ours: 10K mathematics and 2K coding); the 27B run uses 10K mathematics examples. Matching hyperparameters and example counts does not imply matched realized training tokens.

Implementation.

SFT enables padding removal, gradient checkpointing, activation offloading, and resharding after the forward pass; compilation with torch.compile is disabled. GRPO uses dynamic batching for the actor and rollout log-probability computation. The actor keeps parameters and optimizer states on device, while the reference model offloads its parameters. KL regularization is applied through the actor loss, separately from the reward.
